items.question: Who gives the message that he says will happen?

window.31: After burying him, he said to his sons, “When I die, bury me in the grave where the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones.
window.32: For the message he declared by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the towns of Samaria will certainly come true.”

reader.quote: the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones. For the message he declared
reader.contrast: The man of God originally declared the message, while the current speaker says that it will come true.
reader.reason: The window supports the intended answer through the antecedent of “he,” but the question blurs the original declarer with the current speaker. Asking who originally declared the message would recover the intended relation.

editor.quote: the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones. For the message he declared by the word of the Lord against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the towns of Samaria will certainly come true.
editor.contrast: The man of God originally declared the message, whereas the speaker tells his sons that it will come true.
editor.reason: The speaker is a plausible answer because he is the one now saying the message will come true. The generic verb “gives” and the pronoun “he” blur that role with the man of God’s role as the original declarer. Asking who originally declared the message would make the key unique.

items.question: Who mounts the donkey?

window.11: Now there was a certain old prophet living in Bethel, whose sons came and told him all that the man of God had done there that day. They also told their father what he had said to the king.
window.12: Their father asked them, “Which way did he go?” And his sons showed him which road the man of God from Judah had taken.
window.13: So he said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” And when they had saddled the donkey for him, he mounted it
window.14: and rode after the man of God. He found him sitting under an oak tree and asked, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” “I am,” he replied.

reader.quote: And when they had saddled the donkey for him, he mounted it and rode after the man of God.
reader.contrast: The old prophet mounts the donkey, whereas his sons only saddle it for him.
reader.reason: The singular “he” refers to the old prophet who requested the donkey; the sons are the plural “they” who saddle it.

editor.quote: So he said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” And when they had saddled the donkey for him, he mounted it
editor.contrast: The sons saddle the donkey, but their father, the old prophet, mounts it.
editor.reason: The change from “they” to “he” distinguishes the sons who prepare the donkey from the old prophet who rides it.

items.question: Who will kill the priests who make offerings there on that altar?

window.1: By the word of the Lord a man of God came from Judah to Bethel, as Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make an offering.
window.2: By the word of the Lord he cried out against the altar: “Altar, altar! This is what the Lord says: ‘A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who make offerings here, and human bones will be burned on you.’”
window.3: That same day the man of God gave a sign: “This is the sign the Lord has declared: The altar will be split apart and the ashes on it will be poured out.”

reader.quote: A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who make offerings here
reader.contrast: Josiah is the future actor who will kill the priests; Jeroboam is merely present when the prophecy is delivered.
reader.reason: The pronoun “he” refers to the immediately named son, Josiah, and sacrificing the priests entails killing them.

editor.quote: A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David. On you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places who make offerings here
editor.contrast: The future son Josiah is the actor in the prophecy, not Jeroboam, who is merely standing by the altar when it is announced.
editor.reason: Jeroboam is a plausible misreading because he is present at the altar, but the prophecy introduces Josiah and then says that “he” will sacrifice the priests. In this context, sacrificing them entails killing them.

items.question: Whose body is warned will not be buried with family?
items.key: the man of God from Judah

window.20: While they were sitting at the table, the word of the Lord came to the old prophet who had brought him back.
window.21: He cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, “This is what the Lord says: ‘You have defied the word of the Lord and have not kept the command the Lord your God gave you.
window.22: You came back and ate bread and drank water in the place where he told you not to eat or drink. Therefore your body will not be buried in the tomb of your ancestors.’”

reader.quote: the man of God who had come from Judah, “This is what the Lord says: ‘You have defied
reader.contrast: The man of God as the addressee whose body is meant versus the old prophet as the speaker delivering the warning.
reader.reason: The second-person warning is addressed to the man of God from Judah, so “your body” is his. The stem should say “Who is warned that his body…” because a body itself is not warned.

editor.quote: He cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah
editor.contrast: The man receiving the warning versus the old prophet who delivers it.
editor.reason: The old prophet could be confused with the person threatened because the word first comes to him. However, he addresses the man of God from Judah, so the second-person phrase “your body” refers to that man.

items.question: Whom does the king order others to capture?

window.4: When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him!” But the hand he stretched out toward the man shriveled up, so that he could not pull it back.
window.5: Also, the altar was split apart and its ashes poured out according to the sign given by the man of God by the word of the Lord.

reader.quote: When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him!”
reader.contrast: The man of God as the person to be seized versus Jeroboam as the person issuing the order.
reader.reason: The king directs “Seize him!” at the man of God whose proclamation provoked him. This requires resolving the command’s object rather than confusing it with the speaker.

editor.quote: When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him!”
editor.contrast: Jeroboam gives the order, while the man of God is the person the order targets.
editor.reason: The king is the speaker and points toward the man of God when ordering others to seize “him,” resolving the pronoun’s reference.

items.question: Why does the man of God refuse the king’s offer?
items.key: Because the word of the Lord commanded him.

window.8: But the man of God answered the king, “Even if you were to give me half your possessions, I would not go with you, nor would I eat bread or drink water here.
window.9: For I was commanded by the word of the Lord: ‘You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.’”
window.10: So he took another road and did not return by the way he had come to Bethel.

reader.quote: For I was commanded by the word of the Lord: ‘You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.’
reader.contrast: The Lord’s command causes the refusal; the offer of half the king’s possessions is a hypothetical concession, not the reason.
reader.reason: “For” introduces the man’s stated reason, while “even if” shows that a larger offer would not change his refusal. The question tests that causal and concessive relationship.

editor.quote: For I was commanded by the word of the Lord
editor.contrast: The Lord’s command is the reason for the refusal; the amount of the king’s offer is only part of a rejected hypothetical.
editor.reason: The man of God explicitly introduces the Lord’s command as his reason. Saying “even if” the king offered half his possessions rules out the offer’s size as the cause.

items.question: According to the claim, who is to eat and drink?

window.18: The old prophet answered, “I too am a prophet, as you are. And an angel said to me by the word of the Lord: ‘Bring him back with you to your house so that he may eat bread and drink water.’” (But he was lying to him.)
window.19: So the man of God returned with him and ate and drank in his house.

reader.quote: Bring him back with you to your house so that he may eat bread and drink water.
reader.contrast: The man of God is to eat and drink; the old prophet is instructed to bring him back.
reader.reason: In the alleged angelic message, “him” and “he” refer to the man of God. However, “According to the claim” is an avoidably generic reference and should identify the old prophet’s alleged message.

editor.quote: So the man of God returned with him and ate and drank in his house.
editor.contrast: The man of God as the intended eater and drinker versus the old prophet who reports the claim.
editor.reason: The old prophet is plausible because he voices the claim and owns the house, but the third-person “him” and “he” refer to the person he is addressing. The following action confirms that this is the man of God.

items.question: Who prays when the king asks for help?

window.6: Then the king said to the man of God, “Intercede with the Lord your God and pray for me that my hand may be restored.” So the man of God interceded with the Lord, and the king’s hand was restored and became as it was before.
window.7: The king said to the man of God, “Come home with me for a meal, and I will give you a gift.”

reader.quote: So the man of God interceded with the Lord
reader.contrast: The king requests prayer, while the man of God performs it.
reader.reason: The passage explicitly assigns the intercession to the man of God, not to the king who asks for help.

editor.quote: So the man of God interceded with the Lord
editor.contrast: The man of God who prays versus the king who requests the prayer.
editor.reason: The king is a plausible alternative because he asks for help and is the beneficiary. The next sentence explicitly makes the man of God the one who intercedes, so the key uniquely identifies the praying agent.

items.question: Where does the prophet take the body first?

window.26: When the prophet who had brought him back from his journey heard of it, he said, “It is the man of God who defied the word of the Lord. The Lord has given him over to the lion, which has mauled him and killed him, as the word of the Lord had warned him.”
window.27: The prophet said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me,” and they did so.
window.28: Then he went out and found the body lying on the road, with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. The lion had neither eaten the body nor mauled the donkey.
window.29: So the prophet picked up the body of the man of God, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back to his own city to mourn for him and bury him.
window.30: Then he laid the body in his own tomb, and they mourned over him and said, “Alas, my brother!”

reader.quote: brought it back to his own city to mourn for him and bury him. Then he laid the body in his own tomb
reader.contrast: The first destination is the prophet’s city, not the tomb where he subsequently lays the body.
reader.reason: The sequence explicitly says that the prophet brings the body to his city before placing it in his tomb.

editor.quote: brought it back to his own city to mourn for him and bury him. Then he laid the body in his own tomb
editor.contrast: The body is taken to the city first and placed in the tomb afterward.
editor.reason: The tomb is a plausible later destination, but the explicit sequence establishes the prophet’s own city as the first destination.

items.question: Who is killed by the lion on the road?

window.23: When the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey for him.
window.24: As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him, and his body was left lying on the road, with both the donkey and the lion standing beside it.
window.25: Some people who passed by saw the body lying there, with the lion standing beside the body, and they went and reported it in the city where the old prophet lived.

reader.quote: When the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey for him. As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him, and his body was left lying on the road, with both the donkey and the lion standing beside it.
reader.contrast: The departing man of God is killed; the prophet who saddled the donkey for him is not the victim.
reader.reason: The prophet prepares the donkey for the man of God, after which the beneficiary goes on his way and is killed. The question tests resolution of the male pronouns between the two men.

editor.quote: When the man of God had finished eating and drinking, the prophet who had brought him back saddled his donkey for him. As he went on his way, a lion met him on the road and killed him
editor.contrast: The reader must resolve whether the departure and subsequent death concern the man of God or the prophet who had brought him back.
editor.reason: The nearby prophet makes the pronouns initially ambiguous, but he prepares the donkey for the man of God, who then goes on his way; the old prophet remains associated with the city where the death is reported.

items.question: What does Jeroboam not do?

window.33: Even after this, Jeroboam did not change his evil ways, but once more appointed priests for the high places from all sorts of people. Anyone who wanted to become a priest he consecrated for the high places.
window.34: This was the sin of the house of Jeroboam that led to its downfall and to its destruction from the face of the earth.

reader.quote: Jeroboam did not change his evil ways
reader.contrast: Jeroboam does not change his evil ways, but he does appoint priests again.
reader.reason: The reader must preserve the sentence’s negation rather than confuse what Jeroboam fails to do with what he actually does.

editor.quote: Jeroboam did not change his evil ways
editor.contrast: Jeroboam fails to change his ways, whereas appointing priests is something he does again.
editor.reason: The passage explicitly negates changing his evil ways and then contrasts that failure with his renewed appointment of priests.

items.question: Who commands the 307,500 trained men?

window.11: Uzziah had a well-trained army, ready to go out by divisions according to their numbers as mustered by Jeiel the secretary and Maaseiah the officer under the direction of Hananiah, one of the royal officials.
window.12: The total number of family leaders over the fighting men was 2,600.
window.13: Under their command was an army of 307,500 men trained for war, a powerful force to support the king against his enemies.
window.14: Uzziah provided shields, spears, helmets, coats of armor, bows and slingstones for the entire army.
window.15: In Jerusalem he made devices invented for use on the towers and on the corner defenses so that soldiers could shoot arrows and hurl large stones from the walls. His fame spread far and wide, for he was greatly helped until he became powerful.

reader.quote: The total number of family leaders over the fighting men was 2,600. Under their command was an army of 307,500 men trained for war
reader.contrast: The 2,600 family leaders command the army, whereas Jeiel and Maaseiah are involved in mustering and organizing it.
reader.reason: “Their” refers to the immediately preceding family leaders, making them the commanders of the 307,500 men.

editor.quote: The total number of family leaders over the fighting men was 2,600. Under their command was an army of 307,500 men trained for war
editor.contrast: The 2,600 family leaders command the army, while Jeiel and Maaseiah are involved in mustering it.
editor.reason: Jeiel and Maaseiah are plausible because they are named in connection with organizing the army. The explicit phrase “Under their command,” however, refers to the immediately preceding 2,600 family leaders.

items.question: Which person do Azariah and eighty priests follow into the temple?

window.16: But after Uzziah became powerful, his pride led to his downfall. He was unfaithful to the Lord his God, and entered the temple of the Lord to burn incense on the altar of incense.
window.17: Azariah the priest with eighty other courageous priests of the Lord followed him in.
window.18: They confronted King Uzziah and said, “It is not right for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord. That is for the priests, the descendants of Aaron, who have been consecrated to burn incense. Leave the sanctuary, for you have been unfaithful; and you will not be honored by the Lord God.”

reader.quote: Azariah the priest with eighty other courageous priests of the Lord followed him in. They confronted King Uzziah
reader.contrast: Uzziah is the person being followed, while Azariah and the eighty priests are the followers.
reader.reason: The priests follow “him” and then confront that same person, explicitly identified as King Uzziah.

editor.quote: Azariah the priest with eighty other courageous priests of the Lord followed him in. They confronted King Uzziah
editor.contrast: King Uzziah as the person followed versus Azariah as one of those doing the following.
editor.reason: The priests follow “him” after Uzziah enters the temple, and their confrontation identifies that person as King Uzziah.

items.question: Who teaches Uzziah to revere the Lord?
items.key: Zechariah teaches Uzziah to revere God.

window.3: Uzziah was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years. His mother’s name was Jekoliah; she was from Jerusalem.
window.4: He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, just as his father Amaziah had done.
window.5: He sought God during the days of Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God. As long as he sought the Lord, God gave him success.

reader.quote: Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God.
reader.contrast: Zechariah instructed Uzziah, whereas Amaziah is identified as the father whose good conduct Uzziah followed.
reader.reason: The relative clause directly identifies Zechariah as Uzziah’s instructor, distinguishing that role from Amaziah’s role as his father and example.

editor.quote: Zechariah, who instructed him in the fear of God
editor.contrast: Zechariah instructs Uzziah, whereas Amaziah is the father whose right conduct Uzziah follows.
editor.reason: Amaziah is a plausible distraction because he is named as Uzziah’s example, but the relative clause explicitly identifies Zechariah as his instructor. The question tests the distinction between an instructor and a model.

items.question: Why is Uzziah eager to leave?
items.key: Because the Lord had afflicted him

window.19: Uzziah, who had a censer in his hand ready to burn incense, became angry. While he was raging at the priests in their presence before the incense altar in the Lord’s temple, leprosy broke out on his forehead.
window.20: When Azariah the chief priest and all the other priests looked at him, they saw that he had leprosy on his forehead, so they hurried him out. Indeed, he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.

reader.quote: Indeed, he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.
reader.contrast: Uzziah is eager to leave because of the Lord’s affliction, not merely because the priests are hurrying him out.
reader.reason: The passage explicitly attaches Uzziah’s eagerness to the Lord’s affliction with “because.” This distinguishes the stated cause from the priests’ simultaneous response.

editor.quote: Indeed, he himself was eager to leave, because the Lord had afflicted him.
editor.contrast: The reader must distinguish the stated reason for Uzziah’s eagerness from the priests’ separate act of hurrying him out.
editor.reason: The priests’ action is a nearby possible cause of his departure, but the passage explicitly attributes his eagerness to the Lord’s affliction.

items.question: For what purpose do the people of Judah take Amaziah's son?
items.key: To make him king in his father Amaziah’s place.

window.1: Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
window.2: He was the one who rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after Amaziah rested with his ancestors.

reader.quote: took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
reader.contrast: Making Uzziah king is the purpose of taking him; Amaziah’s death is the surrounding succession circumstance.
reader.reason: The sentence directly connects the people’s taking Uzziah with making him king in his father’s place.

editor.quote: made him king in place of his father Amaziah
editor.contrast: Making Uzziah king is the purpose of taking him, whereas Amaziah’s death is a surrounding circumstance rather than the stated purpose.
editor.reason: The first sentence directly links taking Uzziah with making him king in his father’s place.

items.question: Whose love of soil explains the farm work?

window.9: Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, at the Valley Gate and at the angle of the wall, and he fortified them.
window.10: He also built towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns, because he had much livestock in the foothills and in the plain. He had people working his fields and vineyards in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.

reader.quote: He had people working his fields and vineyards in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.
reader.contrast: Uzziah’s love motivates the farm work, not the workers’ love of the soil.
reader.reason: The pronouns “his” and “he” continue to refer to Uzziah, and “for” links his love of the soil to having people work his land.

editor.quote: He had people working his fields and vineyards in the hills and in the fertile lands, for he loved the soil.
editor.contrast: The singular owner, Uzziah, loves the soil; the people are those he has working his land.
editor.reason: The pronouns continue to refer to Uzziah, the passage’s singular subject, rather than to the plural workers.

items.question: Whom does God help Uzziah against in battle?
items.key: The Philistines, the Arabs in Gur Baal, and the Meunites.

window.6: He went to war against the Philistines and broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod. He then rebuilt towns near Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines.
window.7: God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabs who lived in Gur Baal and against the Meunites.
window.8: The Ammonites brought tribute to Uzziah, and his fame spread as far as the border of Egypt, because he had become very powerful.

reader.quote: God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabs who lived in Gur Baal and against the Meunites.
reader.contrast: The Philistines, Arabs, and Meunites are opponents against whom God helps Uzziah; the Ammonites are instead described as bringing tribute.
reader.reason: The repeated phrase “against” explicitly identifies all three opponent groups. Distinguishing them from the separately mentioned Ammonites requires tracking the groups’ different relationships to Uzziah.

editor.quote: God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabs who lived in Gur Baal and against the Meunites.
editor.contrast: The peoples Uzziah was helped against versus the Ammonites, who brought him tribute.
editor.reason: The Ammonites are a plausible mistaken inclusion because they are named immediately afterward, but the passage explicitly limits God’s help against opponents to the Philistines, the Arabs in Gur Baal, and the Meunites. The Ammonites have the distinct role of bringing tribute.

items.question: What happens after Uzziah is buried?

window.21: King Uzziah had leprosy until the day he died. He lived in a separate house—leprous, and banned from the temple of the Lord. Jotham his son had charge of the palace and governed the people of the land.
window.22: The other events of Uzziah’s reign, from beginning to end, are recorded by the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
window.23: Uzziah rested with his ancestors and was buried near them in a cemetery that belonged to the kings, for people said, “He had leprosy.” And Jotham his son succeeded him as king.

reader.quote: Uzziah rested with his ancestors and was buried near them in a cemetery that belonged to the kings, for people said, “He had leprosy.” And Jotham his son succeeded him as king.
reader.contrast: Jotham’s succession follows the burial, whereas Isaiah’s recording of the reign is mentioned earlier.
reader.reason: The narrative places Jotham succeeding Uzziah immediately after the account of Uzziah’s burial.

editor.quote: Uzziah rested with his ancestors and was buried near them in a cemetery that belonged to the kings, for people said, “He had leprosy.” And Jotham his son succeeded him as king.
editor.contrast: Jotham succeeding Uzziah after the burial versus Isaiah recording Uzziah’s reign before the burial is narrated.
editor.reason: The sequence places Jotham’s succession immediately after Uzziah’s burial. Isaiah’s recording is mentioned earlier.

items.question: Who is ordered to be killed by the sword?

window.15: Jehoiada the priest ordered the commanders of units of a hundred, who were in charge of the troops: “Bring her out between the ranks and put to the sword anyone who follows her.” For the priest had said, “She must not be put to death in the temple of the Lord.”
window.16: So they seized her as she reached the place where the horses enter the palace grounds, and there she was put to death.

reader.quote: put to the sword anyone who follows her
reader.contrast: The followers are the stated targets of the sword command, rather than the woman who is brought out and later executed.
reader.reason: The command explicitly applies “put to the sword” to anyone following the woman. Her later death creates a credible confusion, but she is not the grammatical object of that particular command.

editor.quote: put to the sword anyone who follows her.
editor.contrast: The woman is ordered to be brought out, whereas anyone following her is explicitly ordered to be put to the sword.
editor.reason: The command assigns different actions to the woman and her followers. Although the woman is later put to death, the explicit sword command applies uniquely to her followers.

items.question: Who is instructed to protect the temple on the king’s behalf?
items.key: the two companies that normally go off Sabbath duty

window.4: In the seventh year Jehoiada sent for the commanders of units of a hundred, the Carites and the guards and had them brought to him at the temple of the Lord. He made a covenant with them and put them under oath at the temple of the Lord. Then he showed them the king’s son.
window.5: He commanded them, saying, “This is what you are to do: You who are in the three companies that are going on duty on the Sabbath—a third of you guarding the royal palace,
window.6: a third at the Sur Gate, and a third at the gate behind the guard, who take turns guarding the temple—
window.7: and you who are in the other two companies that normally go off Sabbath duty are all to guard the temple for the king.
window.8: Station yourselves around the king, each of you with weapon in hand. Anyone who approaches your ranks is to be put to death. Stay close to the king wherever he goes.”

reader.quote: you who are in the other two companies that normally go off Sabbath duty are all to guard the temple for the king
reader.contrast: The two companies going off duty are assigned to guard the temple, while the three companies going on duty receive other specified posts.
reader.reason: The quoted instruction directly assigns guarding the temple for the king to the two companies that normally go off Sabbath duty.

editor.quote: You who are in the three companies that are going on duty on the Sabbath—a third of you guarding the royal palace, a third at the Sur Gate, and a third at the gate behind the guard, who take turns guarding the temple— and you who are in the other two companies that normally go off Sabbath duty are all to guard the temple for the king.
editor.contrast: The reader must determine whether the temple-guarding command applies only to the two off-duty companies or to both the three on-duty and two off-duty companies.
editor.reason: The two-company reading is plausible because that group appears immediately before the command. However, the sentence coordinates the three companies with the other two and says they are “all” to guard the temple. The key is therefore incomplete; changing it to include both groups would repair the item.

items.question: Between whom is the first covenant Jehoiada makes?
items.key: the Lord, the king, and the people

window.17: Jehoiada then made a covenant between the Lord and the king and people that they would be the Lord’s people. He also made a covenant between the king and the people.
window.18: All the people of the land went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed the altars and idols to pieces and killed Mattan the priest of Baal in front of the altars. Then Jehoiada the priest posted guards at the temple of the Lord.

reader.quote: Jehoiada then made a covenant between the Lord and the king and people that they would be the Lord’s people. He also made a covenant between the king and the people.
reader.contrast: The first covenant includes the Lord, king, and people; the second includes only the king and people.
reader.reason: The two successive covenants have different parties, so identifying the first requires keeping their order and participants distinct.

editor.quote: made a covenant between the Lord and the king and people that they would be the Lord’s people.
editor.contrast: The first covenant includes the Lord, king, and people; the second is only between the king and people.
editor.reason: The passage names two covenants in sequence, so identifying the first requires keeping their participants distinct.

items.question: Who remains hidden with Ahaziah's son's nurse for six years at the temple?

window.1: When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she proceeded to destroy the whole royal family.
window.2: But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Jehoram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the royal princes, who were about to be murdered. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom to hide him from Athaliah; so he was not killed.
window.3: He remained hidden with his nurse at the temple of the Lord for six years while Athaliah ruled the land.

reader.quote: took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the royal princes, who were about to be murdered. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom to hide him from Athaliah; so he was not killed. He remained hidden with his nurse at the temple of the Lord for six years
reader.contrast: Joash remained with his nurse; Ahaziah was Joash’s deceased father, not the person in hiding.
reader.reason: The repeated pronouns refer back to Joash son of Ahaziah, whom Jehosheba hid with his nurse.

editor.quote: took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the royal princes, who were about to be murdered. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom to hide him from Athaliah; so he was not killed. He remained hidden with his nurse at the temple of the Lord for six years
editor.contrast: Joash, Ahaziah’s surviving son, remains hidden with the nurse; Ahaziah himself is already dead.
editor.reason: Ahaziah is a plausible misreading because the question names him possessively, but the opening establishes that he is dead. Joash is then named as his son, and the subsequent pronouns identify Joash as the person hidden with his nurse.

items.question: Who gives the spears and shields to the commanders?
items.key: Jehoiada the priest gives the weapons.

window.9: The commanders of units of a hundred did just as Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each one took his men—those who were going on duty on the Sabbath and those who were going off duty—and came to Jehoiada the priest.
window.10: Then he gave the commanders the spears and shields that had belonged to King David and that were in the temple of the Lord.

items.question: Who do the people trample at the entrance?

items.question: What must happen before the ambushers act?
